content: Recurrent episodic wheezing associated with viral upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) is a distinct clinical condition that differs from persistent atopic asthma. The purpose of this review was to determine whether corticosteroid treatment, administered either episodically or daily, is beneficial for children experiencing episodic viral wheeze. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing corticosteroid treatment to placebo in children under 17 years of age who had episodic viral wheeze. This condition was defined as wheezing occurring alongside cold-like symptoms (coryzal symptoms) with minimal or no symptoms of lower respiratory tract involvement between episodes. The primary outcome assessed was the need for oral corticosteroids during episodes, while secondary outcomes included episode severity, frequency, duration, and parental treatment preference. Five RCTs involving children with a history of mild episodic viral wheeze were identified. Most of these children had not required frequent oral corticosteroids in the past and had very few hospital admissions. Three studies focused on preschool-aged children who were treated with episodic high-dose inhaled corticosteroids (1.6–2.25 mg per day). Two of these studies used a crossover design, while one used a parallel design. Additionally, two studies evaluated maintenance low-dose inhaled corticosteroids (400 micrograms per day) in children. One of these studies involved preschool-aged children, while the other included children aged 7–9 years. The results from the two crossover studies of episodic high-dose inhaled corticosteroids demonstrated a reduced need for oral corticosteroids during episodes (Relative Risk [RR] = 0.53, 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.27–1.04). In these two double-blind studies, parents preferred this treatment over placebo (RR = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.48–0.87). However, maintenance low-dose inhaled corticosteroids did not show a clear reduction in the proportion of episodes requiring oral corticosteroids (RR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.23–2.90) or hospital admissions (RR = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.01–4.11). In conclusion, episodic high-dose inhaled corticosteroids appear to be a partially effective treatment strategy for managing mild episodic viral wheeze in children. However, there is currently no evidence to support the use of maintenance low-dose inhaled corticosteroids for the prevention or management of this condition.
